items.prompt:
(1) Which property distinguishes a gas from a liquid?
A. Fills all available space
B. Occupies a measurable volume
C. Contains particles in motion
D. Has a measurable mass [1]

(2) Why can a perfume spread through still air after evaporating?
A. A net flow of air is essential
B. Perfume travels until molecular motion stops
C. Molecules move only down a pressure gradient
D. Random motion spreads perfume molecules [1]

(3) What does nucleon number count?
A. Protons and electrons
B. All particles in the atom
C. Neutrons and electrons
D. Protons and neutrons [1]

(4) Which statement correctly relates isotopes to radioactivity?
A. Isotopes are all naturally radioactive
B. Radioactivity removes an outer-shell electron
C. Isotopes may be stable or radioactive
D. Different mass numbers require different elements [1]

(5) A supplied table places X in Group I and Y in Group VII. Which prediction best fits their positions?
A. X forms X⁻; Y forms Y⁺
B. X forms X⁺; Y forms Y⁻
C. X forms X²⁺; Y forms Y²⁻
D. X forms X⁻; Y forms Y⁻ [1]

(6) Why is helium very unreactive under ordinary conditions?
A. Its first electron shell is full
B. It has the same electron count as neon
C. Its nucleus does not attract outer electrons
D. It needs six more electrons for stability [1]

(7) Why can brass have different copper-to-zinc proportions in different products?
A. Brass is a variable-composition mixture
B. Brass is a variable-formula compound
C. Cooling changes atoms into new elements
D. Copper and zinc require fixed proportions [1]

(8) Which attraction is responsible for a covalent bond?
A. Nuclei attracting other positive nuclei
B. Electrons attracting other negative electrons
C. Nuclei attracting a shared electron pair
D. Molecules attracting neighbouring neutral molecules [1]

(9) Which electron arrangement correctly describes neutral NH3?
A. Three N–H bonds and two nitrogen lone pairs
B. Two N–H bonds and no lone pairs
C. Three N–H bonds and one nitrogen lone pair
D. Four N–H bonds and no lone pair [1]

(10) What is the molecular shape of water?
A. Tetrahedral
B. V-shaped
C. Linear
D. Pyramidal [1]

(11) Why does graphite withstand very high temperatures despite its layers sliding readily?
A. Sliding layers require breaking every covalent bond
B. Strong covalent bonds remain within each layer
C. Interlayer attractions exceed the bonds within layers
D. Graphite consists of separate carbon molecules [1]

(12) Which pairing correctly matches a structure with its bonding model?
A. Copper: alternating positive and negative copper ions
B. Diamond: separate molecules held by weak intermolecular forces
C. Sodium chloride: positive ions in a sea of electrons
D. Chlorine molecule: a shared electron pair between two atoms [1]
items.canonical_answer:
(1) A. Fills all available space. A gas expands to fill its container; a liquid retains a fixed volume.
Distractor explanations: B: Liquids also occupy measurable volumes. C: Particles move in liquids as well as gases. D: Liquids also have measurable mass.

(2) D. Random motion spreads perfume molecules. Random molecular motion produces net diffusion from higher to lower concentration.
Distractor explanations: A: Diffusion occurs even without bulk airflow. B: Molecules continue random motion after they have spread. C: Diffusion does not require a pressure gradient.

(3) D. Protons and neutrons. Nucleons are the protons and neutrons in the nucleus.
Distractor explanations: A: Electrons are not nucleons; neutrons are missing. B: Electrons are outside the nucleus and are not counted. C: Protons are missing and electrons should not be counted.

(4) C. Isotopes may be stable or radioactive. Isotopes describe nuclear composition; radioactivity concerns instability and decay.
Distractor explanations: A: Some isotopes have stable nuclei. B: Radioactivity is a nuclear change, not simply loss of an outer electron. D: Isotopes of one element have the same proton number but different mass numbers.

(5) B. X forms X⁺; Y forms Y⁻. The main-group outer-electron patterns favour loss of one electron by X and gain of one by Y.
Distractor explanations: A: Group I atoms normally lose one electron; Group VII atoms gain one. C: The common charges for these groups are one, not two. D: X normally loses an electron and becomes positive.

(6) A. Its first electron shell is full. A complete first shell accounts for helium’s low tendency to gain, lose or share electrons.
Distractor explanations: B: Helium has two electrons; neon has ten. C: Its positive nucleus does attract its electrons. D: The first shell is full at two electrons, not eight.

(7) A. Brass is a variable-composition mixture. Alloy composition can vary because the components are mixed rather than fixed in one compound formula.
Distractor explanations: B: Brass is an alloy mixture, not a compound with a chemical formula. C: Cooling does not change nuclei into different elements. D: Fixed composition is characteristic of compounds, not brass mixtures.

(8) C. Nuclei attracting a shared electron pair. Positive nuclei attract the negative shared electrons.
Distractor explanations: A: Two positively charged nuclei repel. B: Two electrons repel because both have negative charge. D: Intermolecular attractions do not constitute the covalent bond within a molecule.

(9) C. Three N–H bonds and one nitrogen lone pair. Three shared pairs plus one lone pair complete nitrogen’s outer shell using the available eight outer electrons.
Distractor explanations: A: Three bonds and two lone pairs give nitrogen too many outer electrons for neutral NH3. B: NH3 requires three N–H bonds and a nitrogen lone pair. D: Four N–H bonds describe ammonium bonding, not neutral NH3.

(10) B. V-shaped. The H–O–H arrangement is bent or V-shaped.
Distractor explanations: A: Tetrahedral describes methane molecular geometry, not the three atoms in water. C: Water is bent because of its bonding and lone-pair arrangement. D: Pyramidal describes ammonia, which has three bonded hydrogens.

(11) B. Strong covalent bonds remain within each layer. Sliding involves weaker interlayer attractions, while strong intralayer covalent bonds require much energy to break.
Distractor explanations: A: Layers can slide without breaking the covalent network inside each layer. C: Interlayer attractions are weaker than intralayer covalent bonds. D: Graphite has extended covalent layers, not separate small molecules.

(12) D. Chlorine molecule: a shared electron pair between two atoms. Cl2 contains a single covalent bond.
Distractor explanations: A: Copper has positive metal ions and delocalised electrons, not negative copper ions. B: Diamond is a giant covalent network, not separate molecules. C: Sodium chloride has positive and negative ions, not metallic bonding.
marking_guidance: Part 1: Correct option A (1). A. Fills all available space. A gas expands to fill its container; a liquid retains a fixed volume. Distractor explanations: B: Liquids also occupy measurable volumes. C: Particles move in liquids as well as gases. D: Liquids also have measurable mass. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 2: Correct option D (1). D. Random motion spreads perfume molecules. Random molecular motion produces net diffusion from higher to lower concentration. Distractor explanations: A: Diffusion occurs even without bulk airflow. B: Molecules continue random motion after they have spread. C: Diffusion does not require a pressure gradient. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 3: Correct option D (1). D. Protons and neutrons. Nucleons are the protons and neutrons in the nucleus. Distractor explanations: A: Electrons are not nucleons; neutrons are missing. B: Electrons are outside the nucleus and are not counted. C: Protons are missing and electrons should not be counted. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 4: Correct option C (1). C. Isotopes may be stable or radioactive. Isotopes describe nuclear composition; radioactivity concerns instability and decay. Distractor explanations: A: Some isotopes have stable nuclei. B: Radioactivity is a nuclear change, not simply loss of an outer electron. D: Isotopes of one element have the same proton number but different mass numbers. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 5: Correct option B (1). B. X forms X⁺; Y forms Y⁻. The main-group outer-electron patterns favour loss of one electron by X and gain of one by Y. Distractor explanations: A: Group I atoms normally lose one electron; Group VII atoms gain one. C: The common charges for these groups are one, not two. D: X normally loses an electron and becomes positive. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 6: Correct option A (1). A. Its first electron shell is full. A complete first shell accounts for helium’s low tendency to gain, lose or share electrons. Distractor explanations: B: Helium has two electrons; neon has ten. C: Its positive nucleus does attract its electrons. D: The first shell is full at two electrons, not eight. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 7: Correct option A (1). A. Brass is a variable-composition mixture. Alloy composition can vary because the components are mixed rather than fixed in one compound formula. Distractor explanations: B: Brass is an alloy mixture, not a compound with a chemical formula. C: Cooling does not change nuclei into different elements. D: Fixed composition is characteristic of compounds, not brass mixtures. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 8: Correct option C (1). C. Nuclei attracting a shared electron pair. Positive nuclei attract the negative shared electrons. Distractor explanations: A: Two positively charged nuclei repel. B: Two electrons repel because both have negative charge. D: Intermolecular attractions do not constitute the covalent bond within a molecule. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 9: Correct option C (1). C. Three N–H bonds and one nitrogen lone pair. Three shared pairs plus one lone pair complete nitrogen’s outer shell using the available eight outer electrons. Distractor explanations: A: Three bonds and two lone pairs give nitrogen too many outer electrons for neutral NH3. B: NH3 requires three N–H bonds and a nitrogen lone pair. D: Four N–H bonds describe ammonium bonding, not neutral NH3. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 10: Correct option B (1). B. V-shaped. The H–O–H arrangement is bent or V-shaped. Distractor explanations: A: Tetrahedral describes methane molecular geometry, not the three atoms in water. C: Water is bent because of its bonding and lone-pair arrangement. D: Pyramidal describes ammonia, which has three bonded hydrogens. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 11: Correct option B (1). B. Strong covalent bonds remain within each layer. Sliding involves weaker interlayer attractions, while strong intralayer covalent bonds require much energy to break. Distractor explanations: A: Layers can slide without breaking the covalent network inside each layer. C: Interlayer attractions are weaker than intralayer covalent bonds. D: Graphite has extended covalent layers, not separate small molecules. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 12: Correct option D (1). D. Chlorine molecule: a shared electron pair between two atoms. Cl2 contains a single covalent bond. Distractor explanations: A: Copper has positive metal ions and delocalised electrons, not negative copper ions. B: Diamond is a giant covalent network, not separate molecules. C: Sodium chloride has positive and negative ions, not metallic bonding. No mark for more than one selected option.

items.prompt:
(a) Calculate the neutron count in a sodium atom with proton number 11 and nucleon number 23. [1]

(b) Describe the electron transfer when sodium atoms react with chlorine atoms to form sodium chloride. [2]

(c) Explain why solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity. [2]

(d) Explain the bonding and conductivity of sample X from these supplied observations: it melts at a high temperature, does not conduct as a solid, and conducts when molten. [3]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Neutrons = 23 − 11 = 12.

(b) Each sodium atom loses one electron to form Na⁺. Each chlorine atom gains one electron to form Cl⁻.

(c) The ions are charged, but they are held in fixed positions in the solid lattice and cannot move through it to carry current.

(d) X has an ionic lattice. Strong electrostatic attractions require much energy to overcome, giving a high melting point. When molten, its ions can move and carry current.
marking_guidance: Part a: 12 neutrons (1); electron count is not subtracted.
Part b: Sodium loses one electron and forms Na⁺ (1).
Part b: Chlorine gains one electron and forms Cl⁻ (1).
Part c: Ions are the charged particles (1).
Part c: They cannot move through the solid lattice (1); do not credit “there are no charges”.
Part d: Ionic structure inferred (1).
Part d: Strong attractions linked to high energy/melting point (1).
Part d: Mobile ions in the melt carry current (1); do not substitute electrons.

items.prompt:
(a) Draw a circuit for comparing conductivity using a 3 V current-limited DC supply, a switch, an ammeter and two graphite electrodes in a sample beaker. Label the components; the electrodes must not touch. [3]

(b) Describe a method for comparing aqueous sodium chloride with sugar solution using the low-voltage apparatus. Include how the observations are recorded and how contamination between samples is reduced. [3]

(c) Explain these observations: a copper strip conducts; solid sodium chloride does not; aqueous sodium chloride conducts; sugar solution does not. Identify the charge carriers where present. [3]

(d) Describe improvements to this method: the electrode gap changes between solutions, immersion depth is not fixed, and the supply is changed from 3 V to 6 V for the second solution. Link each improvement to the comparison. [3]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) A single series circuit connects supply, switch, ammeter and two separated graphite electrodes dipping into the sample. The sample completes the path between electrodes. See the labelled reference circuit in visuals/VIS-6117-2-circuit.svg.

(b) Test each solution with the same voltage, electrode spacing and immersion depth. Record the ammeter reading in a results table for each named sample. Switch off between tests and rinse electrodes with deionised water, removing residual rinse water before the next sample.

(c) Copper conducts through mobile delocalised electrons. Aqueous sodium chloride conducts through mobile ions, whereas the ions in solid sodium chloride are fixed. Sugar dissolves as neutral molecules, so its solution has no appreciable concentration of mobile ions from the sugar and gives negligible current in this test.

(d) Fix electrode spacing with a holder so the current path length is comparable. Mark and maintain immersion depth so the electrode contact area is comparable. Keep the supply at 3 V so a changed driving voltage cannot explain the different response.
marking_guidance: Part a: Supply and switch in a complete series path (1).
Part a: Ammeter correctly in the path (1).
Part a: Two separated electrodes contact the sample and complete the path through it (1).
Part b: Test the named solutions using the apparatus (1).
Part b: Record the ammeter reading against each sample in a table (1).
Part b: Rinse electrodes between samples to avoid contamination (1); switching off is required safe procedure.
Part c: Mobile electrons in copper (1).
Part c: Mobile ions in aqueous NaCl, distinguished from fixed solid ions (1).
Part c: Neutral sugar molecules give no appreciable ionic conduction in this test (1).
Part d: Fixed spacing linked to comparable current path (1).
Part d: Fixed depth linked to comparable contact area (1).
Part d: Same 3 V supply linked to a fair electrical comparison (1).
